\chapter{El viaje guiado}
\label{ch:es-guia}
\hlchaptermodality{463}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can arrange or join an organised outing: say who is putting it on, that a guide is coming, and ask whether an early start matters to anyone.}

Read the message or notice this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[organizar]{organizar — to put it together}

\label{lesson:ES-C463-organizar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la agenda} and \textbf{encargar}. Somebody has to put the whole thing together, and that is the verb next.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: organizar}
\textbf{organizar} — to organise, to arrange, to put on.

\emph{Organizar una excursión} — to arrange a trip. \emph{Lo organiza el ayuntamiento} — the town hall is putting it on. \emph{Organízate} — get yourself sorted.

\textbf{La organización} is both the act and the body that does it, the same double sense as \emph{la instalación}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the z that becomes c}]
You met this with \emph{rechacé}. Here it is as a rule you can apply everywhere:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{I did it} \\
\midrule
organizar & organi\textbf{c}é \\
empezar & empe\textbf{c}é \\
rechazar & recha\textbf{c}é \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Spanish almost never writes \textbf{ze} — outside a short list of oddities like \emph{zeta} and \emph{zigzag} — and in a verb ending it never does. Wherever an ending would put an \emph{e} after the \emph{z}, the \emph{z} becomes a \textbf{c}, and the sound does not change at all, because \emph{z} and \emph{c}-before-\emph{e} are the same sound already.

It is a spelling rule and nothing more, which is why every \emph{-zar} verb in the language obeys it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Greek \textbf{órganon}, a tool or an instrument — from \emph{érgon}, \textbf{work}.

So an \emph{organ} is a \textbf{working part}, and to organise is to arrange the working parts so they function together. The body's \textbf{órganos} are named the same way: each one is a tool doing a job.

\emph{Érgon} is worth keeping, because it is in English \textbf{energy} (work within), \textbf{surgery} — through \emph{kheirourgía}, hand-work — and \textbf{ergonomic}. And the musical organ is the same Greek noun: an instrument, a tool for making sound.

Spanish took the word from Greek by way of Latin, which is why it kept its shape rather than wearing down.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the boss is organising a trip
  \item I organised it, in the past
  \item what an \emph{órgano} and a tool have in common
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To organise? (\textbf{Organizar}.) I organised? (\textbf{Organicé} — z becomes c.) What does \emph{érgon} mean? (\textbf{Work}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el guía / la guía]{el guía / la guía — the person, and the book}

\label{lesson:ES-C463-guia}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la guardia} and \textbf{seguir}. The first taught you a rule about articles, and the word coming next obeys it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el guía / la guía}
\textbf{el guía} — the guide, the person. \textbf{la guía} — the guidebook, and also a woman doing the job.

\emph{El guía habla inglés} — the guide speaks English. \emph{Una guía de Madrid} — a guidebook. \emph{La guía telefónica} — the phone book.

\textbf{Guiar} is the verb: \emph{nos guió por el casco viejo} — she led us round the old town.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the pattern you already met}]
The duty-chemist lesson gave you this: the feminine names the thing, the masculine names a person. Here is the set again, with the new one in place:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{feminine} & \textbf{masculine} \\
\midrule
la guardia — the watch & el guardia — the officer \\
la guía — the guidebook & el guía — the guide \\
la policía — the force & el policía — the officer \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{La guía} complicates it, because a female guide is \emph{la guía} as well — so the feminine covers both the object and a woman doing the job, and only context separates them. \emph{La policía} does the same: it is the force, and it is also a policewoman. \emph{Llamé a la guía} is almost certainly a person; \emph{compré la guía} is certainly a book.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
A Germanic word — and nobody can tell you which one. The usual candidate is a reconstructed \textbf{*witan}, to watch over, to show the way, which gave Occitan \emph{guidar} and from there \emph{guiar}. The asterisk is the warning you met on \emph{tripaliare}: inferred, never written down. The Academy prefers a different Gothic form again. All the accounts agree on Germanic, and on \textbf{watching}.

So not \emph{one who knows}, tempting as English \textbf{wit} makes it — that is the neighbouring branch, knowing and watching being two limbs off one root for \emph{seeing}. The Germanic \emph{w-} does surface as \textbf{gu-}, as in \emph{guardar} and \emph{guerra}.

Set it against \textbf{seguir}, which is Latin \emph{sequi}, to follow. A \emph{guía} knows the way and a follower \emph{sigue}. Two words for the two ends of the same walk, one Germanic and one Latin — which is the ordinary condition of Spanish vocabulary rather than an oddity.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the guide speaks English
  \item I bought a guidebook
  \item which article makes it a person, and why it is not decisive
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The guidebook? (\textbf{La guía}.) A male guide? (\textbf{El guía}.) What is the root of \emph{guía}? (\textbf{A Germanic word for watching over} — reconstructed, so it carries an asterisk.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[importar]{importar — to matter}

\label{lesson:ES-C463-importar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{importante} and \textbf{interesar}. The first has a verb inside it, and that verb behaves like the second.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: importar}
\textbf{importar} — to matter, to be of concern.

\emph{No importa} — it doesn't matter. \emph{¿Te importa si abro la ventana?} — do you mind if I open the window? \emph{Me importa mucho} — it matters a lot to me.

It also means to import goods, which is the literal sense, but the everyday one is mattering.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: it works like gustar and interesar}]
The thing that matters is the \textbf{subject}, and the person is an indirect object — the same shape as \emph{interesar}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{word for word} \\
\midrule
\emph{me interesa el arte} & art interests me \\
\emph{me importa el resultado} & the result matters to me \\
\emph{no me importan los horarios} & the timetables don't matter to me \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The verb agrees with the \textbf{thing}, not the person: \emph{importan} for plural timetables. English puts the person first and Spanish puts the thing, which is why \emph{I don't mind} comes out as \emph{no me importa} — literally \textquotedblleft{}it doesn't matter to me\textquotedblright{}.

That makes \textbf{¿te importa…?} the standard polite request: you are asking whether a thing would matter to them, not asking permission.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{importare}: \textbf{in-}, in, plus \textbf{portare}, \textbf{to carry}. To carry something \textbf{in}.

Importing goods is carrying them in, and that is the whole of what Rome meant by it. \textbf{Mattering} is the later half, invented inside the Romance languages long after Latin — you met that split under \emph{importante}, and this is the verb it was cut from. A thing that \emph{imports} brings weight in with it.

\emph{Portare} is a wide family: \textbf{transportar}, \textbf{exportar}, English \textbf{portable} and the \textbf{porter} who carries your bags. Keep it apart from its look-alike \emph{porta}, a \textbf{gate} — the word inside \emph{la puerta}, \emph{el puerto} and \textbf{el pasaporte}, which carries you through a gate rather than carrying anything itself. You were warned about this pair at \emph{la puerta}, where English's two \emph{porter}s turned out to be two different words.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item it doesn't matter
  \item do you mind if I open the window?
  \item ask whether the guidebook matters to them
  \item the timetables don't matter to me, watching the agreement
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To matter? (\textbf{Importar}.) What does the verb agree with? (\textbf{The thing, not the person}.) What does \emph{portare} mean? (\textbf{To carry}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(organizar, el guía, importar)]{(organizar, el guía, importar) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R463-repaso-guia}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all three: \emph{to organise}, \emph{the guide}, \emph{to matter}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the verbs where the thing is the subject}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{what is the subject} \\
\midrule
\emph{me gusta el libro} & the book \\
\emph{me interesa el arte} & art \\
\emph{me importa el resultado} & the result \\
\emph{me duele la cabeza} & the head \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Four verbs, one shape, and you now have the four this book has given you — the family is larger, and \emph{encantar}, \emph{faltar} and \emph{parecer} all run on the same machine. The person is never the subject; the thing is, and the verb agrees with it. \emph{Me importan los horarios} takes the plural because the timetables are doing the mattering.

The useful consequence: \textbf{¿te importa…?} is how Spanish asks a small favour, and it is not asking permission. It asks whether the thing would weigh on them.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two spellings the ending forces}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{I did it} \\
\midrule
organizar & organi\textbf{c}é \\
rechazar & recha\textbf{c}é \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Verb endings never put an \textbf{e} after a \emph{z}, so every \emph{-zar} verb swaps to \textbf{c} before an \emph{e}. The sound is unchanged; only the letter moves.

And \textbf{la guía} carries its accent for the reason \emph{la vía} did — to keep the \textbf{i} from fusing with the \textbf{a}. Two syllables, not one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item they're organising a trip with a guide
  \item the times don't matter to me
  \item how you would ask somebody if they mind
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
All three again, in Spanish, without looking. Then one sentence arranging an outing.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(la excursión del sábado) — read it, then do it yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C463-sintesis-guia}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{organizar} and \textbf{el guía}. The notice below has one doing the other.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
A message to a walking group. Read it, then answer.

\begin{quote}
Hola a todos. La excursión del sábado la \textbf{organiza} el centro cívico.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Viene un \textbf{guía} del pueblo, así que no hace falta llevar mapa.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Salimos a las ocho. Si a alguien le \textbf{importa} madrugar, hay otro grupo a las once, pero ese no lleva guía.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item who is putting the trip on, and who is coming with it
  \item why you do not need a map
  \item the difference between the two groups
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{La excursión del sábado la organiza el centro cívico} puts the object first and then repeats it as \textbf{la}. That doubling is not a mistake and not emphasis for its own sake: Spanish allows the object to lead the sentence, and when it does, a pronoun must hold its place beside the verb. English would say \textquotedblleft{}the Saturday trip is organised by the civic centre\textquotedblright{} and reach for a passive; Spanish reorders instead.

\textbf{Si a alguien le importa madrugar} is \emph{importar} in its natural habitat. The subject is \emph{madrugar} — getting up early is what does the mattering — and \emph{a alguien le} marks the person it matters to. Word for word: \textquotedblleft{}if getting up early matters to anyone\textquotedblright{}.

Note \emph{le} even though \emph{alguien} is already named. Spanish doubles the indirect object almost always, and leaving the \emph{le} out would sound incomplete.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Four lines to a group: say who is organising the outing, say a guide is coming, give the time, and ask whether an early start matters to anyone.

Then check yourself: did \emph{importar} agree with the thing rather than the person, and did you keep the \emph{le}?
\end{tcolorbox}
